moments.title: The Division of Labour in Society
moments.body:
Durkheim distinguishes mechanical solidarity (similarity-based) from organic solidarity (interdependence-based).

He argues modern societies cohere through specialised, mutually dependent roles.
moments.takeaway: Modernity needs a sociology because it produces a new kind of social bond.

moments.title: Le Suicide
moments.body:
Durkheim shows suicide rates correlate with religion, marital status and wartime, arguing the phenomenon is a 'social fact'.

Later critics (Douglas, 1967) question whether 19th-century coronial records are robust enough to support the analysis.

quote.text: There can be no sociology unless societies exist, and societies cannot exist if there are only individuals.

moments.takeaway: Sociology stakes its independence from psychology by showing patterns no individual story explains.

moments.title: The Elementary Forms of Religious Life
moments.body: Durkheim treats religion as society's reflection on itself, drawing on Aboriginal Australian ethnography (which he himself never conducted).
moments.takeaway: Foundational theory in sociology often relied on second-hand ethnographic sources.

now.title: Sociology of the social bond today
now.body: Contemporary scholars use Durkheimian frameworks to study loneliness, online community and political polarisation. Suicide research integrates sociological and clinical data.
now.open_questions: How do digital platforms reshape integration and regulation? Are anomic conditions identifiable in contemporary data?

items.reflection: Durkheim wrote during the founding of the French Republic; his concerns about social cohesion echo current public debates.

moments.title: The Communist Manifesto
moments.body: Written in London on the eve of Europe's 1848 revolutions, the pamphlet sketches a theory of history as class struggle.
moments.takeaway: Sociological theory and revolutionary politics emerge intertwined.

moments.title: Capital, volume one
moments.body:
Marx analyses commodity exchange, surplus value and the accumulation of capital using British factory data.

Volumes two and three are published posthumously by Engels.
moments.takeaway: Long-form economic analysis grounded Marx's broader sociological framework.

moments.title: Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century
moments.body: Piketty's long-run tax data reopen debates about capital accumulation and inequality, arguing that returns on capital tend to outpace economic growth.
moments.takeaway: Empirical revival of classical questions can reshape contemporary political debate.

now.title: Class analysis today
now.body: Modern stratification research uses occupational, cultural and wealth measures (e.g. Savage et al.'s 2013 'Great British Class Survey'). Wealth taxation is debated in OECD countries.
now.open_questions: How should new asset categories (housing, pensions, digital) be incorporated into class measures? Does globalisation alter class formation?

items.reflection: Marx's predictions about industrial proletariat formation took unexpected paths in different national contexts.

moments.title: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
moments.body:
Weber links the Calvinist concept of the 'calling' to dispositions favourable to capital accumulation in Northern Europe.

His comparative method ranges across world religions.
moments.takeaway: Religion shapes economic behaviour in ways material analysis alone misses.

moments.title: Economy and Society
moments.body: Compiled after Weber's death in 1920, this massive treatise sets out his typologies of authority (traditional, charismatic, legal-rational) and the analysis of bureaucracy.
moments.takeaway: Bureaucratic rationality, for Weber, was both efficient and dehumanising.

now.title: Rationalisation today
now.body: Weber's themes recur in studies of algorithmic management, performance metrics and credentialism. The 'iron cage' metaphor is used to describe contemporary digital and managerial environments.
now.open_questions: Do algorithmic systems extend or transform bureaucratic rationality? Where do charismatic dynamics arise inside legal-rational structures?

items.reflection: Weber's ambivalence about modernity, both admiring and critical, remains a model for sociological writing.

moments.title: Park and Burgess at Chicago
moments.body:
Robert Park, a former journalist, joins Chicago and develops 'human ecology' as a way to study the city.

The department becomes a centre of empirical urban research.
moments.takeaway: The city itself becomes a laboratory for sociological method.

moments.title: The City
moments.body:
The volume sets out concentric-zone theory of urban growth.

Direct-observation studies by graduate students (Thrasher's The Gang, 1927; Wirth's The Ghetto, 1928) populate the framework.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical models gained empirical bite through ethnographic detail.

moments.title: Street Corner Society
moments.body: Whyte's 'Cornerville' study of an Italian-American Boston neighbourhood becomes a methodological landmark in participant observation.
moments.takeaway: Sustained immersion produced descriptions impossible from a survey.

now.title: Urban ethnography today
now.body: Modern urban ethnographers (e.g. Sudhir Venkatesh, Mitchell Duneier) extend the Chicago tradition. Mixed-methods designs combine ethnography with administrative data.
now.open_questions: What protections should ethnographers offer subjects in surveillance-rich environments? How should AI-assisted coding be used?

items.reflection: Many Chicago School studies treated immigrant and Black communities as objects of study without fully engaging with researchers from those communities.

moments.title: Le Deuxieme Sexe
moments.body:
Beauvoir argues 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', framing gender as constructed.

The book influences both philosophy and what would become feminist sociology.
moments.takeaway: Continental philosophy seeded sociological frameworks decades before they entered the discipline.

moments.title: The Sociology of Housework
moments.body: Oakley's interview study of London housewives establishes domestic labour as a topic for sociology in its own right.
moments.takeaway: Naming unpaid labour as 'work' reshaped how the economy was measured.

moments.title: Crenshaw on intersectionality
moments.body: Crenshaw's legal-theoretical concept of intersectionality is published, eventually reshaping social science measurement.
moments.takeaway: Categories that work singly may obscure compound experiences of inequality.

now.title: Gender sociology today
now.body: Contemporary work combines feminist theory with administrative-data analysis (e.g. gender pay gap research). Time-use surveys measure unpaid labour systematically.
now.open_questions: How are gendered patterns shifting in remote-work economies? How should sex/gender categories be operationalised across heterogeneous populations?

items.reflection: Sociology's gender turn took decades to reorganise curricula, even after the underlying scholarship was established.
